label: paragraph_title
text: CLUB NICKNAMES.

label: text
text: HOME SOCCER TIT-BITS.

label: text
text: With the start of a new football season, says a Home paper in mail week, club supporters have been turning out in their tens of thousands ready to cheer—and perchance to jeer—their favourite team. While an interesting story could be told of the origin, history, and name of famous clubs, an even more attractive narrative could be woven around "the manner" in which noted football combinations obtained their nicknames. For a club to receive a nickname which is joyously ejaculated by thousands of perfervid supporters is the hall mark of fame.

label: text
text: Many of the nicknames are, of course, obvious. For instance, the Heart of Midlothian are known all over the country as the Maroons, a name derived from the distinctive jerseys worn by the Tynecastle players. The same applies to Rangers, whose supporters yell at the pitch of their voices:—“Come on, the Light Blues,” a reference to the attractive hue of the Ibrox players' shirts.

label: text
text: There is also a smack of their origin in Third Lanark being dubbed the Warriors, as the club were originally known as the Third L.R.V., and even yet in some parts of Glasgow the Cathkin club are referred to as the Volunteers. Then Partick Thistle are known as the Jags, an obvious term emblematic of the prickly qualities of the Scottish thistle, while the Spiders, the name by which Queen's Park are known far and wide, is derived from the black and white striped jerseys worn by the amateurs of Hampden.

label: text
text: Aberdeen players respond vigorously to the encouraging shouts of their followers when they yell:—"Play up, the Dons," although why the Don should be preferred to the Dee is a mystery to many followers of the game in other parts of the country. But Aberdeen, at least up till recently, used to be greeted as the Wasps on account of the yellow and black striped shirts worn by the players of the Pittodrie club.

label: paragraph_title
text: The Bairns of Falkirk.

label: text
text: Not so obvious, however, to the general football public is the reason why Falkirk F.C. are known as the Bairns. But there is usually some local explanation in such a case, and when it is recalled that a familiar slogan in the Stirlingshire town is "Better meddle with the devil than the pairns o' Falkirk," the nickname applied to the Brockville club becomes apparent.

label: text
text:
Ayr United are known as the Honest Men, presumably on account of the tribute paid by Burns to the Auld Toon, rather than any suggestion that the Somerset Park players are more truthful and honest than other players throughout the country.
It is, however, when we come to consider the nicknames of several famous English clubs that some explanation other than the peculiar colour of their shirts is necessary to account for familiarly shouted exhortations. Hull City are known locally as the Tigers, but there is nothing ferocious about the play of the team in the great Yorkshire seaport. One can rendily understand Aston Villa respondin' to the shouts of the Villans, although the Birmingham club has such a proud record as to discount any suggestion of rascality.

label: text
text: Chelsea players think there is nothing derogatory in the appellation of the Pensioners, while the Toffee Makers, by which nickname Everton are known, is, of course, a reference to the brand of toffee manufactured in the district. There is some reason for New

label: text

label: text
text: Notte: County, known as the Lambs, would scorn any special consideration being shown them on that account. Of course, with Crystal Palace, who are known as the Glaziers, the reason is pretty apparent owing to the vast amount of glass used in the construction of that huge undertaking.

label: text
text: Barnsley, a famous cup-fighting team, are known as the Colliers, and it is fitting a team belonging to the great East Coast fishing port, Grimsby Town, should answer to the nickname of the Mariners, while the Wolves is a handy and easily uttered substitution for the cumbersome Wolverhampton Wanderers. But why are Coventry City known as the Bantams? Surely the Midland team are not composed of players all approximating to the height and weight of Alan Morton!

label: text
text: Millwall answer to the name of the Dockers, and Northampton, the centre of a great bootmaking industry, to that of the Cobblers, and it is not surprising that Norwich City should be familiarly known all over the country as the Canaries. Down South, when anyone refers to the Railwaymen in a football connection, everybody knows that Swindon Town are the team in question on account of the extensive railway works in the district, while Gillingham players readily answer to the name of the Hoppers.

label: text
text: But perhaps the most interesting nickname of the lot is that applied to Bolton Wanderers; who are known far and wide as the Trotters. How came a famous club like the Wanderers to get a name? The explanation, even although I do not vouch for its accuracy, is interesting:

label: text
text: Bolton is not exactly a town of millionaires, and thousands of busy workers used to consider pigs' feet a bit of delicacy, and they were in the habit of walking through the streets gnawing away contentedly at a cooked pig's trotter. But the nickname Trotters must have been given to the Wanderers by some jealous people who do not claim Bolton as their birthplace.

label: text
text:
That the members of Hong Kong's mass meeting were not alone in their opinion. that Canton's challenge to British treaty rights called for immediate and prompt action is shown by editorial comment in the leading Home newspapers and journals at the time news reached there of the embargo on British shipping.
Instancing the need for direct action, the “Telegraph” refers to the “useful, precedent” which America set a few months ago when the American naval commander threatened to use force if there was any attempt to restrict the free navigation of American ships. America in the light of this and more weighty facts could not but approve of the adoption by the British and Japanese of similar measures should the need for it arise.

label: text
text: Discussing the regulations emanating from Canton, the "Telegraph". states:—

label: text
text: The first is clearly designed to prevent steamers of all nationalities, "other than British and Japanese," from touching at Hongkong, under penalty of being denied an entry to Chinese ports. Does this prohibition also apply to the Chinese vessels, mostly junks, to which goods are generally transhipped from British ships at Hongkong for conveyance to Cantonese river and other southern ports? It is difficult to resist the impression that we are here witnessing a deliberate conspiracy to destroy the economic importance of Hongkong as a great commercial distributing and transhipment centre.

label: text
text: The various inquiries and surveys now in progress will enable a decision to be postponed by London for yet a few days, until the whole situation has been cleared up. But it is now admitted that, once the official review thereof has been completed, prompt action will have to be taken. The feeling is also gaining ground that, in such an emergency as this where the exercise of our specific Treaty rights are directly challenged, and may be denied to us by violence, there is no reason why we should consult the dozen Powers or more, whose rights are unaffected. An exchange of views between London, Tokyo, and Washington should suffice.

label: text
text: As a matter of fact, Washington would be unlikely to raise any substantial objections to such naval measures as we and the Japanese may be constrained to take for the protection of British and Japanese merchantmen and merchandise from physical interference by the Canton: "Reds," to judge from an American precedent a few months old. This was during the struggle for mastery at and around Shanghai between Generals Li and Chi, and the defending commander sought to restrict the freedom of foreign vessels, including American, in the estuary. The retort of the American naval commander was that he would not hesitate to frustrate, by force if necessary, any such attempt to restrict the free navigation of American ships. America, in the light of this and other more weighty facts, could not but approve of the adoption by the British and Japanese naval commanders off Cantonese ports of a similar line of conduct, should the need for it arise. For Chinese labour to refuse to unload British vessels is one thing; for the Chinese central or local authorities to enjoin upon Chinese labour such a course would be a totally different thing — a serious and unfriendly act, contrary to the Treaties. As for any physical molestation of our merchants or seamen, the only suitable retort would be the intervention of the British Navy. The British communities in Hongkong and South China have once more appealed to London that our naval forces in China should be strengthened and allowed greater freedom of action.

label: text
text: The serious nature of the crisis in Canton and Hongkong is revealed in messages reaching. London headquarters of firms which trade in the Far East. They indicate that the agitation has now resulted in what is virtually a national rising, and show that British trade has nowadays come to a complete standstill.

label: text
text: In almost every cablegram in the last few days, commercial correspondents are appealing for representations to be made to the British Government not to delay definite action further.

label: text
text: Their unanimous recommendation is that the position will be best dealt with by the Foreign Office immediately sending an eminent person to Perking armed with a measure of authority to negotiate an agreement.

label: text
text:
The Chinese Government's invitation to the projected Customs Conference claims the right for China to demand complete fiscal autonomy. The demand that made will probably still further prolong the exchanges of views on the subject already is not more than between the numerous Treaty Powers.
The view of the British commercial leaders states the Daily Mail is that, whatever policy is adopted by the Foreign Office, it must be one of firmness and the offensive act on such as the Trading of Customs of the Five Months by excluding Chinese shipping. Could be made the all-time value to the total value of the

label: text
text: The trade representatives declare that the want of evidence of the intention of the British Government to act has become exasperating and is depressing morale in Hongkong. "Every day's delay," states one telegram from Hongkong, "results in increasing financial exhaustion."

label: text
text: Reports from Hongkong and Canton state that the daily financial loss being incurred in both places is about £250,000.

label: text
text: Trade correspondents' messages all allude to the unfortunate absence in Britain, where he is on sick leave, of Sir J. W. R. Macleay, the British Minister to Peking.

label: text
text: A representative of "The Daily Mail" was informed that Sir James Macleay hopes to have recovered sufficiently to enable him to return to Peking in about three weeks.

label: paragraph_title
text: COTTON TRADE'S LOSS.

label: text
text: Order for the winter's trade, receivable during the spring and early summer, were completely lost, and most of the order for next summer's trade, which should have been fulfilled by the autumn, and early winter, have been lost also.

label: text
text: The Chinese situation has cost the Lancashire cotton industry, of which China is the second chief market, the whole of next winter's China trade, and the greater part of next summer's trade. Its losses during the last four months are estimated to have been nearly £1,000,000 a month.

label: text
text: Private telegraphic advices received, however, show that, despite the embargo against British ships at Chinese ports, announced by the Canton authorities, many British ships with cargoes of cotton have got into Shanghai and are being unloaded.

label: text
text: Chinese ports are loaded with cotton goods and merchants are unable to effect deliveries.

label: paragraph_title
text: WAR NOT WANTED.

label: text
text: We do not, of course, want to go to war with China, further states the "Daily Mail," or if we can possibly help it with any one of the domestic or alien tyrannies which usurp authority in that distracted country. With the toiling Chinese millions we have no quarrel, and we do not believe they have any hostile feeling towards ourselves; the majority are scarcely aware of our existence. Our difficulty is with the "students" and other Westernised agitators who are stirring up the mobs and rowdies of the cities at the instigation of the Russian Soviet. These persons care little for the sufferings they may bring upon Chinese peasants, by cutting off their chief source of foreign supplies, provided they can inflict loss upon Great Britain and add to the industrial depression in this country.

label: text
text: That they can do so, if they are allowed to maintain, the boycott they have declared, is obvious. China is one of the great markets for British manufactured commodities. For some of these products it is the greatest foreign market of all. It is Lancashire's largest customer for certain classes of cotton goods, and many mills will have to close down if the Far Eastern trade is arrested. Yorkshire will be no less badly hit. A most substantial portion of the worsteds, woollens, and dyed cloths manufactured in Bradford and the neighbourhood has been prepared for China. The woollens alone came to £8,387,000 in 1924, and the total export of these classes of goods for the year was little short of ten millions sterling.

text: VALUABLE "LINK."

label: paragraph_title
text: PATIENCE REWARD:

label: text
text: The Rev. Chapman Andrews, leader of the Third Asiatic Expedition to Mongolia, reports that priceless discoveries have been made of skulls, the discoveries of the dunia dwellers and their culture, also of what might be termed the link between the age of cold blooded reptiles and warm blooded animals through the multituberente lute skull.

label: text
text: The following article is an appreciation of the persistence of the American Museum of Natural History in sending these repeated expeditions to Mongolia, with such eventual rich reward.

label: text
text: The persistence of the American Museum of Natural History in sending repeated expeditions to Mongolia appears to have been richly rewarded. Two years ago Mr. Roy C. Andrews and his scientific colleagues found fossil dinosaurs with their eggs, but this summer they have also found many traces, though no remains as yet, of paluolithic man. The reason why Professor H. F. Osborn has for many years past advocated an exploration of the fossil deposits of Mongolia may be stated very simply. That vast country is a lofty and arid plateau, with no mountains and very few rivers. Consequently, there is a good chance of finding the fossilised remains of animals in a comparatively undisturbed condition. This prediction was confirmed two years ago, when Mr. Andrews, working at a place five hundred miles within the Gobi Desert, came upon the complete skeleton of a dinosaur with the nine eggs that she had just laid before a sandstorm came and buried her. This sand, falling gently, killed but did not crush, and the great reptile, with her eggs, remained slowly fossilising through perhaps ten million years.

label: text
text: In Professor Osborn's view, these Mongolian dinosaurs were ancestors of the still larger land reptiles found in Western America, such as the famous diplodocus that we may see at the Natural History Museum. Indeed, he inclines to regard Mongolian as "a centre of dispersal" of animal life—as the region, that is, where the main kinds or orders developed first, and whence tuoy spread to other parts of the earth. To establish such a during hypothesis we need, of course, infinitely more evidence than is yet available, but the American scientists who have repentedly braved the tigers of the Gobi Desert in the search for fossils have, at any rate, made the theory seem plausible. This summer Mr. Andrews has discovered six mammalian skills—and the remains of a giant rhinoceros, orbitally in strata above those containing the dinosaurs.

label: text
text: But special interest attaches to his finding of arrowheads, spear points, drills, and the like relics of man of the Old Stone Age, because very little is known of man's presence in Mongolia in the remote past, long before the Mongols lived there. Mr. Andrews's finds should throw welcome light on the migrations of those remote ancestors of ours in the Glacial Period, who apparently roamed over the whole earth, since their weapons and tools are much the same wherever they are found; whether in England or Egypt or Turkestan. Thus the New World through Mr. Andrews and his generous porters, is helping to elucidate the earliest history of the Old
